messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas Keane had always seen himself as a steady, practical man, the kind of school principal who could handle a crisis in the hallway, a parent complaint, or a staff breakdown without losing his footing. That certainty was shattered two years earlier, when a routine medical workup turned into a life-threatening illness that landed him in a hospital bed under bright lights, surrounded by the sharp bite of antiseptic and the stale sweetness of alcohol swabs. He remembered the moment when the doctors’ expressions changed and the room seemed to narrow around him; after that, his memory of the worst hours became strangely patchy. When he tried to deliberately go back over what happened, he found he could not access it cleanly, yet an ordinary scent could bring it back with force. The smell of alcohol in a classroom cabinet or a visitor’s hand sanitizer would hit him in the chest and, without a clear picture, he would be flooded by the same terror he felt in the hospital. At other times, a hospital corridor smell or the sight of a medical exam table would produce the opposite kind of memory, one in which his body felt positioned exactly as it had been then, pinned and vulnerable, as if he were again lying there waiting for news.

In the months after discharge, Thomas began arranging his life around those moments. He avoided hospitals, ambulances, and even routine physical examinations, telling himself he would go “when absolutely necessary,” though he delayed until the last possible minute. Before any interaction, even a simple conversation with a parent or a staff member, he rehearsed what he would say over and over, afraid that if he spoke without preparation he would unravel. He also cut off all contact with friends and family, letting calls go unanswered and declining invitations he once would have accepted without hesitation. These habits narrowed his world, but they felt safer than being caught off guard by something that might carry the smell of a clinic or the reminder of what his body had done to him. His avoidance did not stay contained. The more he shut people out and treated every conversation as something to script, the more isolated and tense he became, and the school office itself began to feel like another place full of possible reminders. A parent arriving for a meeting after a dental appointment, or a nurse calling the school about a student, could bring a faint alcohol scent or antiseptic trace into his day, and Thomas would catch himself bracing before he even knew why.

What frightened Thomas most was what these moments seemed to prove about him. He had come to believe that the person he had become was unrecognisable to him, that he could no longer rely on himself, and that his own body was no longer trustworthy. If he felt his heart race in the hallway or sensed a wave of fear before a routine staff meeting, he read it as evidence that he was fragile in a way he had never been before. That appraisal deepened the problem: the more he saw himself as unreliable, the more he rehearsed every exchange and the more completely he withdrew, and the more alone he became, the more unstable he felt. When the memory intruded without warning, sometimes just as an antiseptic smell drifted through a clinic lobby or as he passed an ambulance parked near the school, the emotional intensity returned before any image did, and his conviction that he was altered and unrecognisable hardened again. Even deliberately trying to remember the hospital stay left him frustrated and shaken, because the missing pieces made the experience feel both distant and dangerously unfinished. By the time he agreed to seek help, his PCL-5 score reflected what his colleagues had begun to notice: Thomas was still functioning, but only by shrinking his life into routines, scripts, and absences. He came to treatment hoping he could finally face medical care without feeling trapped inside that bed again, and fearing most that the next smell of alcohol or antiseptic would convince him, once more, that he had never truly come back.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers leading to avoidance and re-experiencing, but it does not clearly state that triggers themselves cause Thomas's negative beliefs or appraisals about himself.

The vignette shows intrusive memory triggered by smells and linked to terror, but it does not state that the memory itself drives his negative appraisals about being fragile, unreliable, or unrecognisable.
